naiṣṭhika-brahmacārin
(‘the ब्रह्मचारिन् [Vedic student] [who remains] steadfast [to his गुरु throughout his life]’)
------------------------------------------
Students residing in the होउसे of the गुरु (gurukula) for pursuing Vedic studies, were of two types: the upakurvāṇa and the naiṣṭhika.
The former stayed for a limited period (like twelve years or even less) and would offer गुरुदक्षिणा (fee or presents) before leaving.
The latter stayed on till their death. They were to remain celibate, serve their गुरु and also pursue their Vedic studies. If the teacher died, they were to serve the teacher’s son or the wife. They were the perpetual students.
Keeping the Vedic fire of the गुरु burning without being put out was one of their sacred duties, apart from Vedic studies and begging for ड़ोओद्. They were also to abjure all luxuries that violate their vows.
Some dharmaśāstra writers opine that physically handicapped persons (like the blind, the crippled) were to remain as naiṣṭhika brahmacārins (perpetual students) though the able-bodied persons too could opt for this life.

naiṣkarmya
(‘state of absence of all karmas or rituals and actions’)
------------------------------------------
This is a technical term generally favoured by the Advaita Vedānta system. In effect, it means the state of जीवन्मुक्ति or लिबेरतिओन् even while living in this body.
Performing karmas (actions or rituals) whether as a matter of duty or because they have been prescribed by the scriptures, is possible only as long as a person is able to see duality brought about by अविद्या or nescience. When अविद्या is destroyed by आत्मज्ञान (knowledge or direct experience of the आत्मन्, the Self) and the whole world including oneself is perceived as one indivisible pure consciousness—sat-cit-ānanda—there is absolutely no scope or possibility of performing any कर्म at all. This state of मिन्द् of the man of realisation is called ‘naiṣkarmya’ or ‘naiṣkarmyabhāva’.
However, it should not be forgotten that performing all actions ordained by the scriptures with the right attitude leads to cittaśuddhi or purification of मिन्द्. It is only the person endowed with such purity of मिन्द् that is fit for practising ज्ञान, ultimately resulting in the destruction of अविद्या which, then, confers the state of नैष्कर्म्य.

Naiṣkarmyasiddhi
------------------------------------------
Scholars of Advaita Vedānta generally recognise four well-known treatises of advaita philosophy as belonging to a special group—the Siddhi group. They are:
Brahmasiddhi of मण्डन मिश्र (A.

-1632)
Naiṣkarmyasiddhi of Sureśvarācārya (8th century A. D.)
Of these, the Naiṣkarmyasiddhi of सुरेश्वर has earned for itself an enviable place in Advaita literature not only because सुरेश्वर was a direct disciple of शङ्कर but also because of its high quality.
Though traditional biographies of शङ्कर consider सुरेश्वर as the same as मण्डन मिश्र after being converted by शङ्कर, modern scholars do not subscribe to this view.
The work is divided into four chapters, the total number of verses being 423. The author himself has supplied the necessary explanations and connections in simple prose wherever necessary. A brief summary of the work may now be attempted here.
First Chapter (100 Verses)
Salutation to the गुरु; अविद्या or nescience, the cause of सṁसार (bondage); कर्म (rituals) cannot remove अविद्या; कर्म is only a preliminary means; ज्ञान (knowledge of the आत्मन्/Brahman) and कर्म can never go together; arguments of opponents demolished.
Second Chapter (119 verses)
Ignorance of the true nature of tvam (jīva or the individual सोउल्) is the real obstacle to realising the identity with tat (Brahman); greatness of महावाक्यस् (of उपनिषद्स्); आत्मन् is different from the body-मिन्द् complex; scriptural authority in support of this; superimposition and desuperimposition by the vision of the reality; plurality is only phenomenal.
Third Chapter (126 verses)
Nescience (avidyā) removable only by the mahāvākya tat tvam asi; its three aspects; what the sentence really signifies; reason cannot give direct experience; however reason helps and the mahāvākya completes the work of removing अविद्या or nescience; अविद्या is inexplicable; repetition of the mahāvākya and meditation help in realisation.
Fourth Chapter (78 verses)
Brief summary of the earlier chapters; quotations from गौडपाद and शङ्कर in support; जीवन्मुक्ति, the liberated सोउल् and the moral law; qualifications and dispositions needed in the students of this treatise; conclusion.
On the whole this work is an excellent treatise of Advaita Vedānta useful for earnest students of Vedānta as also for scholars.
